explain.say: An RCD, a residual current device, is a safety switch that can stop an electric shock in a split second. It checks that current comes back the way it went out.

faq.q: How does an RCD know everything is normal?
faq.a: In a healthy circuit, every bit of current that goes out on the live wire comes back on the neutral. The RCD constantly compares the two, and while they match, it stays on.

faq.q: What happens when current leaks to earth?
faq.a: If someone touches a live part, or water lets current escape, some current flows to earth through them instead of back along the neutral. Now the outgoing and returning currents differ.
Home RCDs usually trip at an imbalance of 30 milliamps, three hundredths of an amp, which is small enough to stop most shocks before they cause serious harm.
asks: What does 30 milliamps mean on an RCD?

faq.q: How fast does an RCD switch off?
faq.a: Within about 40 milliseconds for a large leak, and within 300 milliseconds at its rated leak, much faster than a single heartbeat. That speed is what makes it life-saving.
asks: How quickly does an RCD trip?

faq.q: How is an RCD different from a fuse?
faq.a: A fuse or breaker reacts to too much current, which protects cables from overheating. An RCD reacts to a tiny leak to earth, which protects people from shocks. Many homes have both.
asks: Do I need an RCD if I have fuses?

facts: Household RCDs are typically rated to trip at a 30 milliamp leak.
A 30 milliamp RCD must trip within 300 milliseconds at its rated leak, and within 40 milliseconds at five times that.
